extracted.intended_audience: Stanford inventors (faculty, staff, students) and other university researchers disclosing technologies to the Office of Technology Licensing
extracted.subtask_description: Procedural and evaluative guidance describing the Office of Technology Licensing's workflow from confidential invention disclosure through patenting, marketing, licensing, monitoring, and income distribution, and the inventor's role at each step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure (Invention and Technology Disclosure Form)
rubrics_metrics.description: During disclosure, the inventors provide a description of the technology and an explanation of the critical solution it could provide to benefit society by submitting a confidential Invention and Technology Disclosure Form to OTL. Submitting this information creates a record of the invention (descriptive information), the inventor(s) involved, who sponsored the work, and public disclosures and publications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For inventions coming out of a particular principal investigator's (PI) laboratory, the PI's authorization is required even if the PI is not an inventor. Disclosure is confidential and establishes the official record for subsequent OTL actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manager Assignment and Docketing
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosures received by OTL are logged in, assigned a docket number, and assigned to a specific licensing manager.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The assigned licensing manager is responsible for all actions relating to the docket going forward; docketing creates the tracking reference for evaluation, prosecution, marketing, and licensing activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation — preliminary evaluation criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: The licensing manager will meet with the inventor(s) to discuss the invention and make a preliminary evaluation of manufacturing feasibility, patentability, novelty, potential applications, and possible markets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because patenting an invention is expensive, the licensing manager may decide not to pursue commercialization. If pursued, a preliminary licensing strategy will be developed. Inventors may assist via prior art searches and by suggesting licensing strategies (e.g., exclusive vs. non-exclusive).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior Art Search and Inventor Participation in Evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: At this stage, the inventors may assist in the evaluation by participating with a prior art search.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OTL welcomes inventors’ suggestions for the best strategy for licensing the technology; inventor participation can materially influence decisions about patentability and strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensing Strategy Selection (exclusive vs. non-exclusive)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different inventions require different licensing strategies. For example, a basic new scientific tool that is likely to be widely used is typically licensed on a non-exclusive basis. In contrast, an invention which requires significant investment of resources by a company is typically licensed on an exclusive basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An exclusive license provides the licensee with an incentive to undertake risky capital investments and commit resources required for product development. Inventor input on strategy is solicited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision to File Patent Application (patentability and commercial viability)
rubrics_metrics.description: OTL does not file patent applications for all invention disclosures it receives. The licensing manager must consider the chances that a technology can be successfully patented or licensed before investing in the cost of obtaining patent protection (approximately $30,000 – $45,000 in the U.S. alone).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors that may make an invention difficult to patent include prior publication or insufficient data. Factors that may make an invention difficult to license include a small potential market or high potential development costs. The licensing manager weighs these factors before pursuing patent protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent Application Preparation and Inventor Role in Prosecution
rubrics_metrics.description: If pursuing patent protection is warranted, the OTL licensing manager will work with the inventors and a patent attorney or agent on preparing the patent application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The inventor’s expertise is crucial during filing and prosecution: attorneys may be unfamiliar with the detailed technical contributions that make the invention novel, useful, and non-obvious. Inventors must provide feedback and respond to attorney questions; the attorney will also ask named contributors about their contributions to determine correct inventorship (see Inventorship FAQ).

rubrics_metrics.name: Marketing: non-confidential abstract and inventor involvement
rubrics_metrics.description: OTL markets the technology to companies by preparing a non-confidential abstract that is made available through OTL’s website and sent directly to targeted companies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OTL works with inventors to prepare the abstract and values inventor insight on technical and market feasibility as well as leads for companies. If a company requests additional technical information, OTL usually asks inventors to provide that information, which can be shared under a confidentiality agreement if necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: License Negotiations — terms, flexibility, and startup accommodations
rubrics_metrics.description: If a company shows strong interest, the licensing manager begins license negotiations starting with a license proposal followed by negotiations requiring flexibility and creativity by both parties to arrive at a mutually satisfactory agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: License terms vary depending on technology, market, and company. Startup companies typically cannot afford large initial payments but may compensate with equity and/or payments once products are on the market. The licensing manager negotiates terms; inventors are generally informed and may help evaluate a company's capacity to develop licensed products.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventor Role and Limitations During Negotiations
rubrics_metrics.description: At the negotiations stage, the inventor’s role is limited. The licensing manager will generally inform the inventors when they are negotiating a license agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inventors may be asked to help evaluate a potential licensee's technical/development capability. If an inventor has a potential conflict of interest, he or she will need to participate in a COI review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict of Interest (COI) Review Participation
rubrics_metrics.description: If an inventor has a potential conflict of interest, he or she will need to participate in a COI review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: COI may affect inventor participation in licensing and should be disclosed; OTL coordinates necessary COI review processes as part of negotiations and agreement execution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitoring Licensee Performance
rubrics_metrics.description: After signing a license agreement, the licensing manager monitors the licensee's performance for the duration of the license.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitoring is usually done through periodic financial or development reports required under most license agreements. Both the license terms and the company’s progress reports are generally considered confidential business information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent Income Distribution Policy (royalty & equity sharing rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: After the conclusion of Stanford's fiscal year, Patent Income(s) received by OTL are distributed according to Stanford policy: after deductions for OTL operations and reimbursement of direct expenses, the distributable Patent Income(s) are divided according to specified percentages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For the first $3,000,000 of cumulative distributable Patent Income from a single license: 33.34% to the inventor, 24.66% to the inventor's department (as designated by the inventor), 21.0% to the inventor's school, and 21.0% to the office of the VPDOR. For amounts exceeding $3,000,000, allocation changes to: 33.34% inventor, 14.66% department, 26.0% school, 26.0% VPDOR. Department and School royalties must be used for research or educational purposes only.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allocation Among Multiple Inventors and Multiple-technology Portfolios
rubrics_metrics.description: In the case of multiple inventors, OTL will divide the inventors’ share equally unless all inventors have agreed to a different allocation. In the case of multiple technologies licensed as a portfolio under a single license, OTL allocates earned royalties only to the docket(s) covering the specific revenue-generating product(s) or service(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Revenue is attributed to dockets based on the patent or technology coverage of those products. Inventors on dockets that do not cover the licensed products or services being sold by the licensee will not receive earned royalties from that license, though they may still receive other types of income (such as annual maintenance fees). See Patent Income Distribution Policy Summary of Changes for specifics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amending Licenses
rubrics_metrics.description: Either party can request an amendment to the Agreement at any time during its life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amendments are negotiated by the licensing manager to adapt to changed circumstances as technologies, companies and markets evolve over time.
